source.title: Opponent actor learning (OpAL): modeling interactive effects of striatal dopamine on reinforcement learning and choice incentive

confidence_rationale: Strong computational grounding for how a dorsal-striatal actor implements credit assignment: OpAL extends the classic actor-critic with a DUAL opponent actor (D1/Go and D2/NoGo populations, the direct/indirect pathways) that separately accumulate positive and negative action values, with dopamine gain-modulating each. It unifies learning and choice-incentive effects the standard actor-critic cannot. Directly grounds the direct/indirect-pathway credit-assignment leg of the pull. Confidence 0.74 (not higher) because the opponent-actor refinement is more architecture than REE needs for the FIRST build -- the load-bearing import is 'a dedicated actor with a value-baseline critic', and OpAL's two-channel detail is a second-order enrichment REE may or may not need.
failure_signatures: OpAL's dual opponent actor is a refinement REE does not need to reach for first: the minimal owed build is a single actor + critic baseline. Importing the D1/D2 opponent split prematurely risks re-instantiating the over-elaboration anti-pattern (governance-mass before capability) the graveyard doc warns against.

OpAL is fit to behavioural/pharmacological data (probabilistic RL, effort-based choice, motor-skill learning); it is a model OF dopamine effects, not a demonstration that an artificial agent needs opponent actors to forage. Transfer to REE competence is indirect.

The interactive learning x incentive effects OpAL captures depend on dopamine as a shared gain term across both actor channels -- a single modulator -- which sits in tension with REE's incommensurable-channel commitment if imported literally.

mapping.source_claim_statement: The classical actor-critic architecture, extended: the actor is replaced by a dual opponent-actor system (two striatal populations, mapping to D1/direct/'Go' and D2/indirect/'NoGo' pathways) that differentially specialize in discriminating positive vs negative action values. Dopamine modulates how much each actor component contributes to both learning and choice, unifying documented dopamine effects on RL, effort/incentive, and motor-skill learning in one framework.
mapping.ree_translation: This grounds the credit-assignment internals of the dorsal-striatal actor the V3-EXQ-724 autopsy pointed to. Two imports for the f_dominance_conversion_ceiling build, ranked: (LOAD-BEARING) an actor is a first-class learner with its own value-baseline critic -- OpAL is built on the actor-critic scaffold, reinforcing that action learning is not a bias term; (SECOND-ORDER) the actor itself can be an opponent pair (Go/NoGo, direct/indirect) so positive and negative action-value credit are assigned on separable channels. REE should build the single-actor+critic first (matching V3-EXQ-737) and treat the opponent-actor split as a later enrichment only if single-actor credit assignment proves insufficient -- consistent with the graveyard doc's warning against structure ahead of capability.
mapping.mapping_caveat: OpAL's opponent-actor detail is more architecture than the minimal owed build requires; the honest import is the actor-critic backbone, with the D1/D2 split flagged as an available-but-not-yet-needed refinement. OpAL is fit to dopamine-pharmacology behaviour, not to a foraging-competence recovery, so it motivates the internal structure of the actor rather than proving REE needs it to clear the floor.
mapping.source_context: Algorithmic/computational-model paper (Psychological Review) fit to human and animal data across probabilistic reinforcement learning, effort-based choice, and motor-skill learning; grounded in D1/D2 striatal microcircuit models.

confidence_components.notes: Source quality high (Psychological Review, Frank lab, canonical for striatal RL modeling). Mapping fidelity moderate (0.68): the actor-critic backbone imports cleanly and directly supports the 'action is a first-class learner' thesis, but the opponent-actor refinement is beyond the minimal build and could mislead toward premature elaboration. Transfer risk 0.4 -- it is a model of dopamine's behavioural signatures, one step removed from the competence-recovery question REE is actually asking.
